title: GOP lawmakers blame Sherrill's 'sanctuary' policies after ICE suspect crashes into NJ mayor's wife
description:
Mikie Sherrill’s is getting blasted for her state’s “sanctuary” policies after an illegal immigrant driver fleeing a stop by Immigration and Customs Enforcement crashed into and injured a local mayor’s wife.
The broadside came after ICE officers conducted a targeted operation involving the driver of an Acura on Route 130 in North Brunswick on Sept. 2.
Republican state Sen. Mike Testa similarly seized on the crash to attack restrictions on cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities.
The illegal alien refused to exit the vehicle or comply with lawful commands from ICE officers.
After repeated verbal warnings and due to officer safety concerns, ICE officers relied on their training and attempted to safely remove the illegal alien.
text:
Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s is getting blasted for her state’s “sanctuary” policies after an illegal immigrant driver fleeing a stop by Immigration and Customs Enforcement crashed into and injured a local mayor’s wife.

“This is just the latest in a long line of traffic incidents and vehicular incidents that wouldn’t occur if New Jersey didn’t have our sanctuary status that got codified as soon as Gov. Sherrill came into office,” Republican Assemblyman Paul Kanitra told Fox News Digital.

“We all fought against it. We told them that this would create chaos, and it seems like Democrats are unable to take accountability for their own actions,” the Point Pleasant Beach lawmaker added.

The broadside came after ICE officers conducted a targeted operation involving the driver of an Acura on Route 130 in North Brunswick on Sept. 2.

ICE said they believed the driver to be an illegal immigrant, and he refused orders to get out of the vehicle before officers attempted to remove him.

He then sped away and ran a red light before colliding with a Tesla driven by Dr. Penelope Cohen, wife of East Brunswick Mayor Brad Cohen, according to local accounts.

Penelope Cohen suffered a leg injury and was taken to the hospital, News 12 New Jersey reported. The Acura driver fled on foot before ICE officers apprehended him shortly afterward.

The driver has not been publicly identified. ICE said he was arrested for violating US immigration law and would remain in custody pending removal proceedings.

Kanitra argued that Sherrill and fellow Democrats have failed to recognize a connection between such incidents and the state’s Immigrant Trust Directive.

“Democrats seemingly have an inability to take accountability for their own actions here. They’re unable to even recognize the chaos that they’re creating, and they’re shouting and screaming at everybody else trying to find somebody to blame. It’s somewhat ridiculous,” Kanitra told Fox.

“You kind of reap what you sow,” he added.

Republican state Sen. Mike Testa similarly seized on the crash to attack restrictions on cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities.

Testa said Cape May and Monmouth counties had fought unsuccessfully for the ability to participate in ICE’s 287(g) interagency cooperation program.

“I think it has only emboldened illegal aliens to engage in illegal behavior,” Testa told Fox.

“This illegal alien was stopped lawfully by federal authorities, ran through a red light, fleeing federal authorities and unfortunately ran into the mayor of East Brunswick’s wife.”

Sherrill, who became governor in January, signed legislation March 25 codifying New Jersey’s Immigrant Trust Directive, which limits voluntary state and local participation in federal civil immigration enforcement.

The policy generally bars New Jersey cops from stopping, questioning, arresting, searching or detaining someone solely on the basis of immigration status and restricts local participation in federal civil immigration operations.

But the directive does not prohibit New Jersey cops from enforcing state criminal laws, complying with valid judicial warrants and court orders or engaging in specified cooperation involving serious offenders.

The Post has sought comment from Sherrill, ICE, Brad Cohen and Dr. Penelope Cohen.

But in a statement to CBS News ICE said: “ICE law enforcement officers conducted a vehicle stop Sept. 2, during a targeted ICE enforcement operation in North Brunswick, New Jersey. The illegal alien refused to exit the vehicle or comply with lawful commands from ICE officers. After repeated verbal warnings and due to officer safety concerns, ICE officers relied on their training and attempted to safely remove the illegal alien. The illegal alien then proceeded to flee at a high rate of speed and collided with other vehicles.”

The U.S. census, a count of every person in the nation every ten years, helps guide federal funding decisions and is used to determine congressional representation.

text:
The Trump administration published a proposal Wednesday that would no longer count immigrants without legal residency in the 2030 U.S. census. The proposed change would also exclude immigrants in the country under temporary lawful protections.

The U.S. census, a count of every person in the nation every ten years, helps guide federal funding decisions and is used to determine congressional representation. Federal funding, such as assistance programs, is rewarded based on factors including demographic data collected by the decennial census.

According to the United States Census Bureau, 353 federal assistance programs use census data to determine how federal money is distributed, though the bureau itself does not make decisions on federal funding.

If approved, the measure would also affect congressional maps by changing the population count used to determine how many representatives a state may get in Congress.

Included in the proposal is a provision suggesting the removal of demographic questions like sexual orientation, race and ethnicity.

Amid the proposal, advocates and constitutional experts have raised concerns on whether the new proposal violates the Fourth Amendment’s mandate to count the “whole number of persons in each state.”

William Roberts, senior vice president of Rights and Justice at the Center for American Progress, wrote in an online statement the new proposal could make it difficult to enforce the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The law prohibits racial discrimination in voting, and removing the demographic questions could make enforcement more difficult, he added.

“Eliminating questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation strips our government of critical data needed to ensure vital resources are extended to the communities who need them most,” he wrote.

In Florida, earlier fights surrounding census data and representation began last year.

In 2025, Gov. Ron DeSantis announced an effort to correct the 2020 U.S. census, saying he believed Florida was “shortchanged” in Congressional representation.

DeSantis said data in the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2022 Post-Enumeration Survey showed Florida was undercounted by 3.5%.

In Florida, the state with the third largest immigrant population in the country, immigrants make up about 10% of the population, according to the Migration Policy Institute.

He said the state did not make an effort to count immigrants without legal residency in the 2020 census, unlike states such as California. He called the practice of counting immigrants without legal status “unconstitutional.”

The proposal is open to public comment until Oct. 13.

text:
At a time when young people are increasingly exposed to complicated political and social debates, Ian Massaro believes they need something more fundamental: a clear understanding of their rights.

Massaro is the founder of KidsKnowRights, a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping young people understand their legal rights through accessible, practical, and nonpartisan education. And unlike many organizational founders, Ian is still in high school.

“I’m in my final year of high school. I’m still in the education system,” he explained. Yet while many students his age are focused on school, friends, and preparing for college, Ian was thinking about a problem he saw around him: young people often do not know what rights they actually have.

KidsKnowRights was formally solidified as an organization in 2024, growing out of Ian’s realization that there was a gap in the organizations serving young people. He had already been involved with other organizations, including New Sanctuary Coalition, which works with people seeking asylum. Through that work, he encountered a teenager around his age who was discouraged because he believed he could not obtain a driver’s license because he did not have immigration documents.

Ian explained to him that, in New York, immigration status does not determine the right to obtain a driver’s license in the way his friend had assumed.

“He didn’t know that,” Ian recalled. “And do you know what that brought him? A happiness that I had never seen in my life.”

That experience stayed with him. For Ian, something as ordinary as being able to drive represented a significant step toward independence and participation in everyday life. The fact that another young person did not know whether he was legally allowed to do something so basic made Ian recognize a much larger problem.

“I saw that there was a failure in the system,” he said.

Rather than simply joining another organization, Ian decided to create one himself.

“When you’re part of another organization, there will always be things that could be improved,” he explained. “As a founder, I can really address the ideas that matter to me and create something that is apolitical.”

That principle is central to KidsKnowRights. Ian emphasizes that the organization is intentionally separate from political parties and political ideology. The goal is not to tell young people what to think, but to help them understand what the law actually says.

“The primary thing is the well-being of kids,” he said.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Kids Know Rights (@kidsknowrights)

Rights Belong to Every Young Person

Ian’s personal connection to immigration also helped shape the organization’s mission. His parents are immigrants, and they frequently told him stories about their early years in the United States, when they did not understand their rights.

“It took 20 years in this country for them to finally understand” what their rights were, he said.

For Ian, that experience reinforced the importance of making legal information accessible much earlier in life.

Today, KidsKnowRights focuses primarily on young people, regardless of immigration status.

“It doesn’t matter if they have documents, if they were born in the United States, or if it’s their first day in the United States,” Ian said. “The reality is that every kid who is in this country has rights, and they need to know them.”

That philosophy is reflected in the organization’s educational materials, which translate complicated legal concepts into language that young people can understand and apply to everyday situations.

From School Backpacks to Interactions with Police

The issues KidsKnowRights addresses are both practical and, at times, highly consequential.

Among the organization’s most important areas of focus are interactions with police and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), particularly because fear can prevent people from asking questions or asserting their rights.

But Ian also emphasizes the importance of everyday situations at school.

For example: What happens when a teacher asks to search a student’s backpack?

Ian believes that young people need to understand the difference between respecting authority and blindly complying with authority.

“A lot of times, when someone in authority tells us something, we don’t question it. We just do it,” he explained. “But when it comes to our rights, it’s important not to always say yes just because you’re saying yes. It’s saying yes while knowing your rights.”

If a student knows they have the option to say no and chooses to comply, that is their decision. The problem, Ian argues, is when a young person says yes simply because they did not know they had a choice.

“That is a serious failure,” he said, describing one of the gaps KidsKnowRights hopes to address.

The organization also tackles controversial subjects by focusing on legal facts rather than political opinions. Abortion, for example, is addressed by explaining where it is legal, under what circumstances, and what options or requirements may apply to adolescents.

“We focus only on demonstrating the facts without opinion,” Ian said.

Other topics include student privacy, interactions with police and school security, workplace rights for teenagers, immigration and family preparedness, digital privacy, peaceful protest and civic participation, and finding trusted adults and legal support.

The organization’s growing library now includes twelve standalone lessons designed to be accessible to young people. Each lesson is intended to take roughly 10–15 minutes and ends with a printable pocket card that young people can keep with them.

Making Legal Information Accessible

For Ian, accuracy is just as important as accessibility.

KidsKnowRights develops its materials through a multi-step process. A writer begins by researching a topic using multiple sources. The article is then independently researched and reviewed by a team of approximately four or five editors. The organization also draws on educational resources and professors with expertise in legal studies.

But Ian sees professional legal review as one of the organization’s most important areas for future development.

“We’re still in the process of finding attorneys who can confirm [the information] with their bar number,” he explained. In other words, KidsKnowRights wants attorneys who are willing to put their professional expertise behind the accuracy of the material.

That has proven difficult for a young nonprofit with limited financial resources.

“Lawyers like money,” Ian said candidly. “We, as an organization, can’t provide that.”

His goal is eventually to build relationships with five or ten attorneys—or more—who can help review the organization’s growing body of material. He hopes that as KidsKnowRights expands its reach and impact, there will be greater incentive for legal professionals to contribute their expertise.

Ian is also interested in engaging law students, particularly those in advanced stages of their education who may be looking for meaningful volunteer opportunities.

Reaching Young People Where They Are

Creating accurate information is only half the challenge. The other half is getting people to use it.

Ian says KidsKnowRights spent roughly its first two years building the organization before beginning to see significant impact in 2026. Partnerships have been critical to that growth.

The organization has worked with churches and community institutions because these organizations already possess something extremely valuable: trust.

“If people trust another organization, they extend that trust to us,” Ian explained.

One of KidsKnowRights’ early presentations took place at Saint Peter’s Lutheran Church in Manhattan. From there, Ian began to see how community partnerships could create a snowball effect. Someone discovers a resource they trust, shares it with a friend, and that person shares it with someone else.

Social media has amplified that process.

Ian and his social media manager have focused particularly on Instagram and TikTok, the platforms where many young people spend their time. Together, the organization’s social media accounts have reached approximately 50,000 followers, with some posts receiving hundreds of thousands of views. Ian says the website now receives approximately 50,000 visitors per month.

Yet the social media strategy is ultimately designed to bring young people toward deeper resources.

“A TikTok or Instagram post isn’t enough,” Ian explained. “I can tell you that on TikTok and Instagram, I watch a video for 30 seconds, and if it doesn’t get to the point, I leave.”

The organization’s website and app therefore serve as the primary home for its more detailed educational materials, while social media helps attract attention to the issues and resources that matter most.

Nonpartisan Does Not Mean Silent

KidsKnowRights’ commitment to being apolitical does not mean avoiding difficult or politically charged subjects.

In September, for example, hundreds of students in Colorado reportedly walked out of school to protest ICE. KidsKnowRights did not tell students whether they should participate in the protest. Instead, it provided information so that students could understand their rights if they chose to participate.

“We’re not political,” Ian emphasized. “But we provide materials to all students so they know what their rights are when they walk out of class to protest.”

That distinction—between advocating a political position and educating people about their legal rights—is fundamental to the organization’s identity.

Building Trust Through Community Partnerships

Churches are an especially important part of Ian’s expansion strategy.

His reasoning is straightforward: when people need help, they often turn to institutions they already trust.

“When you need help, you go to church. You always trust your church,” he said.

KidsKnowRights is therefore seeking partnerships with religious institutions as well as schools and other community organizations. The organization has presented at Ian’s own school and is exploring opportunities to work with New York City Public Schools, although Ian acknowledges that working within a large public-school system can be slow and bureaucratic.

He views each new partnership as building credibility that makes the next partnership easier.

“Every church we work with makes the next one easier,” he explained. His long-term vision is that after building relationships with ten churches, finding the eleventh might take only a few minutes.

The objective is not simply to increase the number of partnerships, but to cultivate credibility so that communities take the organization’s educational materials seriously.

Measuring Impact One Person at a Time

For a young founder, one of the most difficult questions is also one of the simplest: Is it actually working?

Website traffic, social media views, downloads, and other numbers provide one measure of reach. But Ian admits that these numbers do not necessarily tell him whether someone actually used the information when it mattered.

“When I go to sleep, I think about whether I really made an impact or whether I’m just creating numbers that sound nice,” he said.

Ultimately, he has come to define success in more personal terms.

He has spoken with people who received KidsKnowRights’ materials and told him that they actually used them in situations similar to those described in the organization’s courses.

“If there is at least one person in the country that I helped, that’s more than enough for me,” Ian said. “And if we can help 50,000 a month, I’d be even happier.”

For Ian, impact begins with individual victories.

“We can confirm that there is one person we helped,” he said. “And that is more than enough for us.”

A Vision Bigger Than KidsKnowRights

When asked about his ultimate dream for the organization, Ian did not describe a specific number of users or a fixed organizational structure. Instead, he described something broader: a society in which people know that help and rights-based resources exist when they need them.

“I want everyone to know about the opportunities that exist in rights,” he said.

He does not believe every person will necessarily use those resources. What matters is that people who want or need to use them know that they exist.

Ian plans to study public policy when he enters college, with the goal of understanding how he can create tangible social impact and use what he learns to expand KidsKnowRights.

His long-term vision is ambitious.

He imagines an organization where he is no longer responsible for managing every detail and can instead focus on interviews, strategy, and broader outreach.

“I want it to become this monster that I can no longer control,” he said, describing an organization large enough to operate with hundreds of volunteers and professionals.

At the heart of that vision is a simple idea: connecting people who can help with people who need help.

“There is so much polarization in our society,” Ian reflected. “If we could simplify everything to people who can help and people who need help, this country would be much better, and as a society we would be much happier.”

Ian acknowledges that such a vision may never be completely achievable. “I’m a little pessimistic in that sense,” he admitted.

But that does not stop him from trying.

“I want to at least do my part to help, and for people to receive my help.”

A Mission Built Around Knowledge and Empowerment

At its core, KidsKnowRights is built around a deceptively simple premise: young people cannot exercise rights they do not know they have.

Ian’s personal experiences—as the child of immigrants, as a student, and as a young person who has encountered other young people confused about their legal rights—have shaped an organization that seeks to make legal knowledge understandable, practical, bilingual, and accessible.

The organization’s growing rights library reflects that philosophy. Its lessons cover situations young people may encounter at school, at work, online, in their communities, during interactions with police, and within immigrant families. Rather than telling young people what political position to take, KidsKnowRights seeks to give them the information they need to make informed decisions for themselves.

For Ian, the ultimate goal is not simply to create an impressive website, accumulate followers, or produce educational materials.

It is to make sure that when a young person finds themselves in a situation where their rights matter, they are not left thinking, “I don’t know what I can do.”

They know.

And they know where to turn for help.

KidsKnowRights can be found on Instagram and TikTok as @KidsKnowRights, and Ian encourages people to visit the organization’s website and download its app. Every download, he explains, helps the organization reach more young people and advance its mission: “so that more kids across the country can actually know what their rights are.”

Soledad Quartucci, Ph.D. is the Founder and CEO of Latina Republic, a nonprofit dedicated to deepening understanding between the United States, Latin America, and the Caribbean while amplifying the voices and experiences of communities that are too often overlooked. She holds a Ph.D. in U.S. History, with an emphasis on immigration, and is pursuing a Master’s degree in Clinical Psychology with a Marriage and Family Therapy focus through Pepperdine University’s Aliento Program, which centers the mental health and well-being of Latino families and communities.

As a historian, educator, and storyteller, Soledad is passionate about uncovering little-known stories and highlighting the leaders and community members working to create meaningful change. Through Latina Republic, she seeks to expand visibility of the challenges facing underserved communities while elevating the people and organizations creating solutions, advancing human rights, and strengthening communities across the United States and Latin America.

text:
A song of resistance and unity rose from the front steps of the University United Methodist Church Saturday evening.

It wasn’t particularly loud. There was no shouting. As the crowd harmonized their call and response, it sounded like a church hymn.

“This is for our neighbors who are locked inside,” they sang. “Together we can abolish ICE.”

About 70 community members, advocates and organizers from the Workers’ Center of CNY, the Syracuse Immigrant and Refugee Defense Network, the New York Immigration Coalition, and the Food Chain Workers’ Alliance gathered for a vigil to free a Syracuse worker they say was illegally detained by ICE. The man, Carlos Arreaga, is now being held in the federal detention facility in Batavia, a 1:40 drive west of Syracuse.

With a progress-pride flag emblazoned with the words “All are Welcome!” hung on the church behind them, local organizers and Arreaga’s friends and family made impassioned pleas for his release. As the football game ended up the SU hill from church, streams of cars drove by, with many drivers honking and shouting in support.

On the morning of June 26, Immigration and Customs Enforcement took Arreaga into custody on his way to work “without a warrant or any particular reason,” according to his GoFundMe page. The page was set up by his wife, Amelia, to help cover Carlos’s legal fees and the family’s living expenses now that their sole breadwinner is detained in a facility that has been criticised for overcrowding and poor conditions.

Arreaga has filed for asylum in the U.S. and has been a Syracuse resident and active member of the community for the past eight years, according to the press release for Saturday’s vigil. Organizers said that he was detained illegally and continues to be denied bond, despite an order from a federal judge that he be given a bond hearing.

“We will gather to show community support for Carlos, call for his freedom, and expose the worsening situation at the … federal detention center and the ongoing illegal, warrantless detentions and racial profiling that have contributed to the abductions of over 500 people from Onondaga County since January 2025,” organizers wrote in the press release.

Jim McKeever volunteers with the Syracuse Immigrant and Refugee Defense Network, whose work includes ICE watch and rapid response teams, helping families locate their missing loved ones, and a support hotline. He noted that the organization has been much busier within the last year and a half due to increased ICE activity in the area.

“These are guys trying to feed their families,” McKeever said. “They have working permits. They have open asylum cases. But none of that matters. They’re just profiling people in their cars.”

Several community members who knew Arreaga spoke up on his behalf and letters of support and comments about good character were read aloud. “Carlos was an incredible presence in our neighborhood. A good, solid man who did lots of things for everybody,” one of Arreaga’s neighbors said.

Community member Fiorella Buitron said that attending these events is important because “we have to be united in the struggle and be united in the pain that we feel and pull each other together in solidarity.”

The crowd was left with a call to action to continue coming together as a community, speaking out and advocating for Arreaga’s release. The crowd erupted into applause at Kayla Kelechian’s declaration that they fight to “make sure people have access, make sure people have representation.”

Kelechian, the Upstate New York director of organizing and strategy for the New York Immigration Coalition, spoke about the need for immigration attorneys and immigration services and called on community members and activists to continue contacting their elected officials.

“This is a vigil because I am in grief,” Kelechian said. “Families are in grief. But we fight back.”

After the speakers were finished, everyone in attendance stood together on the steps with their signs chanting “free Carlos.” The chants mixed with the sound of cars continuing to honk in support.

“No one is getting left behind this time,” they sang to close out the event. “We’ll get there together or never get there at all.”

text:
(KRON) — California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the County of Santa Clara further blocked the construction of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility on a 24.5-acre parcel in unincorporated Santa Clara County near Gilroy, county officials announced Saturday.

“We’re hopeful the court’s ruling sends a clear message that this is the wrong process and the wrong place for this facility,” Santa Clara County Counsel Tony LoPresti said in a statement.

The Government Services Administration — responsible for acquiring property for the federal government — leased the land from a private developer to use as a “likely Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) holding facility.”

“From there, the federal government moved to build out the site rapidly and without transparency,” county officials said in a statement.

Bonta and LoPresti filed a lawsuit challenging the construction in June calling it “illegal.” The complaint alleges the developers of the ICE facility have not allowed county investigators to inspect the property during construction and that further use will cause “irreparable harm” to the surrounding community.

“Based on known hazardous waste violations at the Holsclaw Property, and the agricultural

research companies’ failure to complete site closure requirements, the County’s Public Health

Department has concluded that “the contamination of structures, soils, the septic system, and

groundwater at the Holsclaw Property is likely if construction continues before the hazards are

assessed and/or addressed,” the complaint states.

The construction was originally pushed back to Sept. 9.

Saturday evening, Judge Eumi K. Lee of the U.S. District Court granted a preliminary injunction to further push construction and require the federal government to submit a proposed order by Sept. 30 outlining the ruling or relief they want the court to adopt.

“No one is above the law — not even the federal government,” Bonta said in a statement.

title: Fake signatures found on forms to keep inmates in jail for ICE, NC sheriff says
description:
A veteran detention officer at a North Carolina jail is facing 20 counts of felony forgery, after it was determined documents linked to deportations had fake signatures, according to investigators.
The paperwork was used to hold suspected undocumented immigrants in jail for Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, officials said.
“On Friday ... the Guilford County Magistrate’s Office notified the Guilford County Sheriff’s Office of a potentially forged court document submitted by GCSO Detention Officer Michael Diehl,” the sheriff’s office said in a Sept 11 news release.
The suspicious signatures were found on AOC-CR-662 forms, county officials said.
The Guilford County Detention Center is in Greensboro, about a 90-mile drive northeast from uptown Charlotte.

Officer Michael Shaun Diehl Jr., 40, was fired, arrested and released on $5,000 bond, officials said. He had been with the department since 2008.

“It appears that in each of these 20 cases, ICE had issued a detainer based on evidence that the inmate who was the subject of the detainer was in violation of United States immigration law,” the sheriff’s office said.

text:
More than a lakh Indian spouses, largely women, hold EADs

A US district court has set aside an interim final rule issued by the Trump administration in Oct 2025 that ended automatic extensions of employment authorisation documents (EADs). However, the relief is limited only to the seven plaintiffs who had challenged the rule and does not apply nationwide. TOI had earlier reported that seven H-4 visa holders (spouses of H-1B professionals with approved green card applications) had approached the district court, arguing that the abrupt withdrawal of automatic EAD extensions, without public consultation, could lead to widespread job losses amid chronic processing delays at the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). More than a lakh Indian spouses, largely women, hold EADs. A 2016 rule introduced automatic extensions of up to 180 days beyond the expiry of an EAD, allowing eligible spouses to continue working while their renewal applications were processed. In spring 2022, USCIS temporarily increased the extension period to 540 days. The extended period was made permanent from Jan 2025 to prevent employment disruptions caused by processing delays. However, in Oct 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) abruptly ended the automatic-extension mechanism through an interim final rule. The lawsuit had argued that H-4 spouses can apply to renew their EADs only within 180 days of the expiry of their existing work permits. Since an H-4 spouse’s status extension must be filed alongside the H-1B worker’s extension, any delay by the employer in filing the H-1B application can further reduce the dependent spouse’s renewal window. The plaintiffs also pointed to USCIS processing delays that routinely exceed 180 days, arguing that the absence of automatic extensions could make job loss unavoidable for many H-4 EAD holders. In an order dated Sept 10, 2026, the US district court (Central District of California) granted a preliminary injunction in favour of the seven plaintiffs. The court held that DHS had failed to follow the procedure required under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) when introducing the rule. The government had justified the move on national security grounds, arguing that automatic extensions could allow individuals to continue working before background checks and eligibility reviews were completed. Judge David O. Carter held that DHS had not demonstrated the emergency circumstances required to bypass the usual notice-and-comment process. The district court noted that the government already had continuous-vetting mechanisms. It also found that DHS had not adequately considered the interests of H-4 EAD holders, their families and employers. Jonathan Wasden, the immigration litigation attorney representing the plaintiffs, said the ruling rejected both the government’s claimed emergency and its failure to meet the substantive requirements of rulemaking. “This means that the final rule the government has been hinting at in recent months is dead on arrival,” he added. However, in the absence of a nationwide injunction, other H-4 visa holders seeking the same benefits will need to approach the court.

text:
The Supreme Court on Friday dropped a major immigration detention case from its docket in Washington after the Supreme Court was told that New York Governor Kathy Hochul had pardoned the migrant at the centre of the dispute, effectively rendering the Supreme Court controversy moot.

The dismissed Supreme Court immigration detention case, Genalo v. Black, had been framed as a potential landmark on how long the federal government can hold people in mandatory immigration detention without a bond hearing.

More Details on the Appeal

It can be recalled that the appeal was being pursued by the Trump administration and was expected to test the limits of detention powers against constitutional guarantees of due process in the court's upcoming October 2026 term.

The Supreme Court case grew out of the detention of two lawful permanent residents who were held for extended periods while the government tried to remove them. Court records show that one man, identified as Carol Williams Black, was detained for seven months, while the other, identified as 'Keisy G.M.' and later named as Keisy Guerrero Mariano, spent 21 months in immigration custody. Neither was given a bond hearing in which a judge could decide whether continued detention was justified.

In May 2024, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that such unreasonably prolonged detention under Section 1226© of federal immigration law violates due process when it occurs without a bond hearing. The appeals court declined to set a rigid time limit but said detention beyond six months raises serious constitutional concerns and upheld a requirement that the government carry the burden of proving why detention should continue. That decision set binding precedent in New York, Connecticut and Vermont.

The case that reached the Supreme Court involved both Black and Mariano. Black's individual dispute later became moot when his immigration proceedings ended and he left the United States, but Mariano's situation remained live, keeping the broader legal questions before the justices.

Pardon Knocks Out Supreme Court Immigration Detention Case

That changed when Hochul granted Mariano a full pardon on 28 August 2026 for his 2015 second-degree assault conviction. According to the governor's clemency announcement, Mariano was one of six people who received pardons, all of whom had completed their sentences and, in the state's view, 'lived crime-free lives for a significant period of time and have made positive contributions to their communities.'

Mariano's lawyers had already told the Supreme Court that the assault conviction was the sole basis for the removal charge and detention at issue in Genalo v. Black. They argued that if the conviction were fully pardoned, he would no longer be removable on that ground and his case would become moot.

Once the pardon was issued, that prediction effectively came true. With the underlying conviction wiped away for the purposes of the removal charge, there was no longer a live controversy over Mariano's detention for the Supreme Court to resolve.

The dismissal followed a joint move by the Trump administration and Mariano's legal team. Both sides told the court that, in light of the pardon, dismissal was appropriate under the justices' own rules.

'The government has decided to stipulate to the dismissal of these cases under this court's Rule 46.1, with the aim of identifying alternative vehicles, including from the Second Circuit, that would still allow this court to resolve the questions presented during October term 2026,' Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

In other words, the Supreme Court case is over, but the underlying fight about prolonged detention is not. Sauer signalled that the administration would search for another case that raises the same constitutional questions and can be moved quickly onto the Supreme Court's docket.

The solicitor general also pointed to differences between the 2nd Circuit's approach and that of other federal appeals courts on bond hearings for people detained under Section 1226©. The government has cited those conflicting approaches as a reason why the Supreme Court should eventually step in.

The 2nd Circuit's ruling remains in place. Lawful permanent residents and other noncitizens detained for long periods in New York, Connecticut and Vermont retain the right to seek bond hearings once their detention becomes unreasonably prolonged, while people held elsewhere may be subject to stricter rules or none at all. It is an uneven landscape, and the court has chosen not to smooth it out, at least not yet.

Reaction to Hochul's Move and What Comes Next for the Supreme Court

Rights groups welcomed the way this particular Supreme Court immigration detention case ended. The American Civil Liberties Union was among the organisations representing Mariano at the Supreme Court stage, and advocates have long argued that indefinite mandatory detention without a bond hearing offends basic due process principles.

Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan publicly criticised Hochul's decision on X. He argued that by pardoning Mariano, the governor had both prevented his removal on the assault conviction and deprived the Supreme Court of the opportunity to decide the detention questions presented in Genalo v. Black.

What is clear from court filings is that Mariano's lawyers themselves had told the justices that a full pardon would end his removability on the relevant ground and moot the dispute. The Trump administration then accepted that reality and agreed the case should be dismissed, even as it made plain that it wants another vehicle to revisit the same questions soon.

The Supreme Court's brief order does not disturb the 2nd Circuit's May 2024 ruling, nor does it provide any nationwide guidance on when mandatory detention under Section 1226© becomes unconstitutional without a bond hearing. Instead, it leaves the lower court framework intact and resets the clock on the federal government's effort to narrow or overturn that approach.

For migrants detained within the 2nd Circuit, that means the existing due-process protections remain in force. For the Trump administration and its solicitor general, it means going back to the drawing board to locate another case clean enough, and live enough, to persuade the Supreme Court to finally say how long the state can lock people up in this kind of immigration limbo.

text:
WASHINGTON: A federal judge has ruled that a plan by the Trump administration to slash staffing at the federal agency tasked with responding to disasters by 50% was unlawful.

The opinion issued late Friday marked a victory for labor groups who had sued the agency. The labor organization had argued that plans by the Department of Homeland Security violated congressional protections that were designed to safeguard the independence of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

The issue of the FEMA staffing was part of a much larger lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees and other labor groups, pushing back on efforts by the Trump administration to slash the federal workforce.

U.S. District Judge Susan Illston wrote in her opinion that top Homeland Security officials late last year directed FEMA’s leadership to submit a staffing plan that included a 50% staffing cut even though the agency’s own supervisors objected.

“Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” wrote Illston.

The Department of Homeland Security and FEMA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Illston wrote that it was clear that the government violated rules established after 2005’s Hurricane Katrina that put decisions on staffing levels squarely in the hands of FEMA, not the Department of Homeland Security and that prevented DHS from “substantially” reducing the “functions” of FEMA.

Illston didn’t order a specific remedy to carry out her opinion but directed the two sides to meet and decide on a course of relief.

Although FEMA has experienced terminations, the 50% staffing cuts ultimately were not carried out. In recent months, after top leadership changes at FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security, the agency has rehired some staffers who were let go.

FEMA was one of the agencies targeted in the federal government for staff reductions as part of a broad Trump administration plan to reduce the size of government. The embattled agency has been buffeted by mass staff departures, disruptions of grant programs, and delays of disaster aid.

In May, a Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council submitted a final report recommending sweeping changes to how the agency supports states, tribes and territories in disaster.

The final version backed away from the recommendation to cut the FEMA workforce by 50%, which was included in a December 2025 draft reviewed by The Associated Press.

The council instead recommended the agency conduct a “strategic review” to determine “appropriate staffing levels.”

In an August report, the Government Accountability Office said it found the departures of thousands of staff in 2025 resulted in a “loss of institutional knowledge and experienced personnel” and “exacerbated longstanding workforce challenges.”

More than 4,300 employees, or about 17% of FEMA’s workforce, separated from the agency in the 2025 budget year, with over 1,500 through voluntary reductions. The agency also made about 2,900 new hires.

The GAO recently recommended to Congress that it “consider requiring” FEMA to base “significant workforce decisions” on a more strategic planning process.

Without it, the GAO found, “FEMA cannot be assured that the agency is positioned to effectively meet its mission needs.”

text:
LEWISTON — Months after a high-profile and public surge by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Lewiston and Auburn continue to see a high number of arrests by federal agents, immigrant advocates say.

The detainments, like the Sept. 3 arrest of Aderno Pinto Sebastiao while he was returning from lunch to his job at Bangor Savings Bank, have put tremendous stress on immigrant families, according to Ruben Torres, director of advocacy and policy for the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.

“This is impacting so many people’s lives on a daily basis,” said Torres. “This affects how people live their livelihoods. For people who’ve been detained, it’s a complete 180 on your life. Everything you were hoping to do in the next two weeks, in the next six months, is automatically put in pause and on the back burner.”

A recent analysis from the coalition found that ICE apprehended more people this year in Maine than in the past two years combined. Lewiston tied with South Portland with 64 arrests through July 31, the most of any community. Auburn was sixth with 31 arrests.

Data show 73 arrests in Maine in July alone, the second highest monthly total in the past two-and-a-half years. According to Torres, ICE was active in 20 communities in 2024; as of this month, ICE activity has been verified in 50 communities.

And not every interaction or arrest is shown in the data, Torres said.

“We are only capturing a fraction of what’s going on in the state,” he said.

The activity comes as ICE receives tens of billions of dollars — three times its last annual budget — in the most recent funding bill passed by congressional Republicans and signed by President Trump.

In previous comments, a spokesperson for ICE said they had not verified the accuracy of the coalition’s report. The agency is “continuing to go after the worst of the worst” and that it believes many of those arrested have committed crimes.

“They just don’t have a rap sheet in the U.S.,” the spokesperson said. “Further, every single one of these individuals committed a crime when they came into this country illegally.”

Additional inquiries to ICE and Department of Homeland Security regarding the enforcement activity in Lewiston-Auburn were not returned.

According to the coalition’s analysis, about 69% of the immigrants who have been arrested by ICE this year have no criminal convictions or charges.

Sebastiao, an Angolan national, apparently has no criminal record — the federal government said he overstayed his visa, while a judge found he has a pending asylum application and cannot be transferred out of state. Despite the judge’s order, Sabastiao is currently at the Plymouth County Correctional Facility in Massachusetts, according to ICE’s online locator system.

“There’s a real fear because everyday citizens who go to work, pay their taxes, are now the target for enforcement despite the image being presented,” said Torres.

Besides the emotional toll, immigration arrests make it difficult for families to get by financially.

“It also takes away from childcare and puts families in a risky situation where they have to find out how they’re going to afford childcare during the detention process,” said Torres.

He said the coalition used to see bail of $1,000 for individuals detained by ICE. It is now often in the $5,000 to $10,000 range. “That’s not money people have on hand,” said Torres.

The impact goes far beyond the arrested individual and their family, said Panagioti Tsolkas, a spokesperson for the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.

“You can’t unsee members of the community being taken by ICE,” said Tsolkas. “Detainments like this scare communities, scare families. We don’t want people scared to leave their homes because of this organization.”

“A lot of difficult conversations families are having are, ‘This is what happens when dad doesn’t come home. This is what happens when mom doesn’t come home.’ It’s tough on everyone,” said Torres.

However difficult the conversations, Torres said, they are necessary.

“The worst thing you can do is be in the moment, panicked, trying to make a plan. In the heat of the moment, the best thing is a plan so everyone knows what to do.”

Residents anxious about ICE’s presence, Torres and Tsolkas said, should rely on community members and organizations who want to support their immigrant neighbors.

“This is an extremely difficult time,” said Torres. “In these times, community is both a source of strength and a place of refuge. Don’t be afraid to lean on your community, they are here to help.”

“No one should ever feel scared, feel isolated or silenced,” said Tsolkas. “There’s a lot of support out there for these individuals.”

text:
A federal appeals court delivered the Trump administration a second major legal setback in less than two weeks, ruling that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) likely broke federal law by sharing taxpayer addresses with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as part of the administration’s deportation push.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit unanimously upheld a lower-court injunction blocking the IRS’s “Data-Exchange Procedure,” which had already turned over more than 47,000 taxpayer records to immigration authorities.

The three-judge panel — Circuit Judges Cornelia Pillard, Patricia Millett and Robert L. Wilkins, all appointed by former President Barack Obama — found that challengers were likely to prove the program violated Section 6103 of the Internal Revenue Code, the post-Watergate statute restricting when the IRS can disclose tax return information to other federal agencies.

Court details how the program fell short of the law

Writing for the panel in a 32-page opinion, Pillard traced Section 6103 to abuses uncovered after Watergate, when congressional investigators found taxpayer information had been used to target political opponents. Lawmakers responded by restricting the IRS from sharing tax return information unless the requesting agency meets “stringent conditions” under the statute.

The court found that ICE’s request for the last known addresses of roughly 1.28 million people went far beyond what Section 6103 permits.

Judges cited evidence that the IRS processed requests even when ICE’s address fields contained placeholders such as “Unknown Address,” “Failed to Provide” or “NA NA,” despite the requirement that agencies provide a taxpayer’s name and address before obtaining return information.

The panel also found that more than 90 percent of the disclosures resulted from taxpayer-identification-number matching that did not confirm ICE had supplied a valid address. The system required only five or nine digits to appear in the address field, without requiring those digits to form an actual ZIP code.

The panel rejected the government’s argument that a single ICE officer could be “personally and directly engaged,” as required by the statute, in tens of thousands of separate criminal investigations.

Pillard also rejected the administration’s fallback argument that an officer could cross-check dates to verify each case, noting that the Data-Exchange Procedure did not record dates for the addresses it used.

The court further rejected the government’s claim that the procedure was an internal operational matter beyond judicial review. It ruled that the program qualified as reviewable “final agency action” under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Pillard wrote that the IRS was “now on notice twice over” about deficiencies in its 2025 disclosures and warned that the agency and its personnel face “steep civil and criminal consequences for willful disclosure of information in violation of section 6103.”

Reaction from the parties

The Center for Taxpayer Rights, which brought the lawsuit, said in a statement to Newsweek that the ruling upheld the “fundamental right to the confidentiality of taxpayer return information.”

The group added that the IRS and Treasury Department cannot “do end runs around carefully crafted statutory exceptions to confidentiality just because it wants to or thinks it knows better.” It said all U.S. taxpayers “should be relieved by the court’s order.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told Newsweek and Reuters that the agency “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and will “continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal.”

The spokesperson added that the decision “in no way prevents us from doing so.”

A second defeat tied to the midterms

The IRS ruling came six days after the same appeals court declined to pause a separate district court ruling against DHS’s expanded Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system.

The administration wanted states to use SAVE to check voter rolls for noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections.

DHS expanded SAVE after an executive order Trump signed in March 2025 titled “Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections.” The overhaul transformed the system from a tool that verified immigration status for benefits eligibility one record at a time into one capable of bulk searches using Social Security numbers and Social Security Administration records involving U.S.-born citizens.

U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb, presiding over League of Women Voters v. DHS, granted summary judgment to the challengers. She ruled that the SAVE overhaul violated the Privacy Act, the Social Security Act and the Administrative Procedure Act.

The D.C. Circuit declined to stay that ruling while the administration’s appeal proceeds. Solicitor General D. John Sauer responded by filing an emergency application with the U.S. Supreme Court arguing that the district court’s order “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”

The application will first go to Chief Justice John Roberts, who handles emergency applications from the D.C. Circuit and can refer them to the full court.

What comes next

Both disputes involve preliminary rulings rather than final judgments on the merits. However, the D.C. Circuit repeatedly indicated in the IRS case that the challengers are likely to prevail.

The Center for Taxpayer Rights said roughly 43,000 taxpayers whose information was found by both courts to have been unlawfully shared with ICE “must be notified so that they may seek damages against the government for this unlawful disclosure.”

The group said it will monitor whether the administration appeals the ruling or changes its procedures.

The SAVE dispute now awaits action from the Supreme Court. Its outcome could determine how much access state election officials have to federal citizenship-verification tools before voters cast ballots in November.

Reaction to Hochul's Move and What Comes Next for the Supreme Court

Rights groups welcomed the way this particular Supreme Court immigration detention case ended. The American Civil Liberties Union was among the organisations representing Mariano at the Supreme Court stage, and advocates have long argued that indefinite mandatory detention without a bond hearing offends basic due process principles.

Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan publicly criticised Hochul's decision on X. He argued that by pardoning Mariano, the governor had both prevented his removal on the assault conviction and deprived the Supreme Court of the opportunity to decide the detention questions presented in Genalo v. Black.

What is clear from court filings is that Mariano's lawyers themselves had told the justices that a full pardon would end his removability on the relevant ground and moot the dispute. The Trump administration then accepted that reality and agreed the case should be dismissed, even as it made plain that it wants another vehicle to revisit the same questions soon.

The Supreme Court's brief order does not disturb the 2nd Circuit's May 2024 ruling, nor does it provide any nationwide guidance on when mandatory detention under Section 1226© becomes unconstitutional without a bond hearing. Instead, it leaves the lower court framework intact and resets the clock on the federal government's effort to narrow or overturn that approach.

For migrants detained within the 2nd Circuit, that means the existing due-process protections remain in force. For the Trump administration and its solicitor general, it means going back to the drawing board to locate another case clean enough, and live enough, to persuade the Supreme Court to finally say how long the state can lock people up in this kind of immigration limbo.

name: Litigation
title: US Homeland Security Deletes AI Generated Mr Singh Poster After Backlash Over Racial Profiling
description:
The department later said that the “Mr Singh” character was intended to represent Harjinder Singh, the truck driver accused in connection with a fatal Florida Turnpike crash in August 2025.
Sikh and Hindu Groups Condemn Use of ‘Mr Singh’ The use of “Mr Singh” prompted strong reactions from Sikh and Hindu advocacy organisations in the United States.
Sikh organisations have repeatedly documented cases in which Sikhs were targeted because of their turbans, beards or perceived association with Islam.
The use of the character therefore raised a separate intellectual-property issue from the criticism over the “Mr Singh” imagery.
DHS has removed the disputed “Mr Singh” advertisement, while maintaining its broader enforcement campaign.
text:
WASHINGTON - The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has removed an AI-generated social media advertisement that featured a turbaned, bearded man identified as “Mr Singh” and urged him to “self-deport,” following criticism from Sikh, Hindu and Indian-American organisations, lawmakers and others over the imagery and language used in the campaign.

The poster was published on DHS’s official X account on September 9, 2026, as part of the department’s wider immigration-enforcement messaging concerning commercial truck drivers and people it says are unlawfully present or improperly licensed in the United States. The graphic was designed around the Transformers franchise and showed a DHS-branded version of Optimus Prime confronting a brown-skinned, bearded man wearing a head covering. It carried the wording, “America for Americans. Get off our roads; you don’t know how to drive, Mr Singh,” alongside the message “Self-deport or find out.”

The post was subsequently removed by DHS. The department later said that the “Mr Singh” character was intended to represent Harjinder Singh, the truck driver accused in connection with a fatal Florida Turnpike crash in August 2025. That clarification came after the image was widely interpreted as portraying Sikh or Indian truck drivers as a group.

DHS Links Poster to Harjinder Singh Florida Crash

The controversy is connected to the Trump administration’s broader campaign against commercial drivers whom federal authorities consider improperly licensed or otherwise in violation of U.S. immigration or transportation requirements.

Harjinder Singh, 28, was involved in a fatal crash on the Florida Turnpike near Fort Pierce on August 12, 2025. According to Florida Highway Patrol investigators, Singh attempted a U-turn in a semi-truck at an area designated for official use, resulting in a collision with a minivan. Three people in the minivan were killed. Singh was subsequently charged with three counts of vehicular homicide and later faced additional manslaughter charges.

Authorities also said Singh was unlawfully present in the United States at the time of the crash and had obtained commercial driving credentials in California. The circumstances surrounding his licensing became part of a wider political and regulatory dispute over the eligibility of non-citizens to obtain commercial driver’s licences and the enforcement of federal standards governing commercial drivers. The DHS campaign referenced Singh alongside other cases involving commercial drivers. A separate AI-generated video posted by the department included the names of Harjinder Singh, Rajinder Kumar, Bekzhan Beishekeev, Akhror Bozorov and Jasveer Singh in connection with accidents or other incidents cited by the administration.

The department’s subsequent explanation is significant because it indicates that the poster was not officially intended to represent every Sikh or Indian truck driver. However, the graphic itself used the surname “Singh” together with a visual depiction strongly associated by many viewers with Sikh identity, including facial hair and a head covering. That combination became the central point of criticism from community organisations.

DHS also defended its broader enforcement campaign when politicians criticised the advertisement. In responses to critics, the department referred to commercial driving licences issued by states and maintained that its campaign was directed at immigration and public-safety enforcement rather than at a particular religious community.

Sikh and Hindu Groups Condemn Use of ‘Mr Singh’

The use of “Mr Singh” prompted strong reactions from Sikh and Hindu advocacy organisations in the United States.

The Sikh Coalition criticised the imagery and said the campaign reinforced concerns about Sikh Americans being judged or targeted because of their appearance. The organisation noted that Singh is a widely used surname among Sikhs and said millions of Sikhs carry the name.

The Hindu American Foundation also condemned the post and described it as racial and religious profiling. The organisation pointed out that the surname Singh is not exclusive to Sikhs and is also used by Hindus. It called for scrutiny of the federal agency’s use of racialised imagery in an official campaign. Other Hindu and Indian-American organisations also objected to the advertisement. The Coalition of Hindus of North America argued that enforcement should focus on individual violations rather than associating particular surnames or communities with unsafe driving or unlawful immigration status.

The criticism was also taken up by members of Congress and other U.S. political figures. Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi said government agencies should not use a person’s faith, heritage or identity to suggest that they do not belong in the United States. Other Democratic lawmakers and officials, including California Governor Gavin Newsom and Senator Adam Schiff, also criticised the campaign. DHS responded to several of its political critics through its own social media accounts.

The controversy has also been viewed against the history of discrimination experienced by Sikh Americans after the September 11, 2001, attacks. Sikh organisations have repeatedly documented cases in which Sikhs were targeted because of their turbans, beards or perceived association with Islam. The current dispute has therefore extended beyond the individual poster to concerns about how federal immigration messaging portrays minority communities.

Hasbro Objects to Transformers Imagery as DHS Removes Post

A separate issue arose over DHS’s use of imagery based on Transformers, including Optimus Prime.

The poster and related social media material portrayed a DHS-branded version of the well-known character in an immigration-enforcement setting. The campaign used the title “Transformers: Age of Deportations,” a reference to the Transformers film Age of Extinction.

Hasbro, which owns the Transformers brand, subsequently said it had not authorised the use of Optimus Prime in the DHS material. The company stated that it was not involved in the campaign and objected to the use of its intellectual property in the government’s messaging. Hasbro also described Optimus Prime as a character associated with qualities including leadership, compassion and justice.

The use of the character therefore raised a separate intellectual-property issue from the criticism over the “Mr Singh” imagery. The available reporting does not establish that Hasbro granted DHS a licence or other permission to use the character in the campaign.

The removal of the “Mr Singh” post came after the combined criticism from advocacy organisations, lawmakers and others. DHS did not issue a public apology alongside the removal, and the department continued its broader immigration-enforcement messaging concerning commercial drivers and voluntary departure from the United States. The campaign is also linked to the administration’s promotion of the CBP Home programme, which allows certain eligible individuals without lawful status to register their intention to leave the United States voluntarily. The programme has included government-provided travel assistance and an exit incentive.

The dispute over the DHS poster consequently involves several separate issues, federal immigration enforcement, commercial-driver licensing and road safety, the use of AI-generated government communications, concerns raised by Sikh and Hindu organisations over ethnic and religious stereotyping, and the unauthorised use of entertainment intellectual property.

DHS has removed the disputed “Mr Singh” advertisement, while maintaining its broader enforcement campaign. The department’s explanation that the image referred specifically to Harjinder Singh has not ended criticism from community organisations, which have continued to question the decision to use a Sikh-associated name and appearance in official federal messaging.

title: Immigration reporting measure fuels debate over Colorado's role with ICE
description:
A 2021 law blocks employees from providing personally identifiable information to immigration enforcement without a warrant or as part of a criminal investigation.
Walsh called Proposition 81 a “recipe for abuse,” saying it would inevitably lead to racial profiling and the detainment of citizens and legal residents.
Burton Brown disagreed, noting that nothing in Proposition 81 allows profiling or gives ICE agents any authority they don’t have in Colorado.
“Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement,” he said.

text:
A coalition of advocacy groups and several district attorneys rallied outside the Colorado Capitol on Thursday to oppose a ballot measure that, if approved by voters in November, would require state and local law enforcement to cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

Backed by Advance Colorado, Proposition 81 would require local law enforcement agencies to notify Immigration and Customs Enforcement when they charge a person who is in the country illegally with a violent crime or when the individual has previously been charged with a felony. This also applies when the person’s legal status cannot be determined.

Kristi Burton Brown, executive vice president of Advance Colorado, told Colorado Politics that the group is pursuing the measure because state law now bars law enforcement from proactively reporting violent offenders or repeat felons to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

She said that, under a recent state law, an officer faces a fine of up to $50,000 for choosing to report a violent offender to federal authorities. She also noted that other “sanctuary” states, including California and New York, include exceptions in these situations that Colorado does not.

While many have characterized Colorado as a “sanctuary state,” Gov. Jared Polis has pushed back on the label, saying the state “fully cooperates with federal authorities in identifying, apprehending and prosecuting criminals – regardless of immigration status.”

Over the years, Colorado has adopted several laws whose provisions fall under the broad outlines of what constitutes a “sanctuary” state.

Notably, a 2019 law prohibits a law enforcement officer from arresting or detaining an individual solely based on a civil immigration detainer and bars a probation officer or probation department employee from providing an individual’s personal information to federal immigration authorities.

A 2021 law blocks employees from providing personally identifiable information to immigration enforcement without a warrant or as part of a criminal investigation. In 2025, Colorado’s legislators imposed the same restrictions on local government employees as well as judicial and legislative employees.

Some local governments, such as Denver, have also adopted “sanctuary” policies.

Speaking from the Capitol steps Thursday, ACLU Colorado director Olivia Mendoza said approving Proposition 81 would make communities less safe, particularly under the current administration.

“We have seen that since the beginning of the Trump administration’s second term, our communities have been gripped by the fear of ICE’s brutal immigration enforcement, from warrantless arrests to physical brutality to deplorable detention conditions,” she said. “ICE has no place in our state, and Amendment 81 invites them to take a strong foothold in Colorado.”

Mendoza argued that Proposition 81 violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits the government from taking away an individual’s life, liberty or property without fair legal proceedings.

Burton Brown countered that the allegations that the measure violates due process are unfounded because law enforcement would be allowed to report to ICE only after obtaining enough evidence to charge someone with a crime.

If the measure passed, it would require law enforcement to contact ICE every time they charge someone who has a prior criminal record, unless that person happened to have proof of citizenship with them in the form of a birth certificate or passport, according to Denver District Attorney John Walsh.

Walsh called Proposition 81 a “recipe for abuse,” saying it would inevitably lead to racial profiling and the detainment of citizens and legal residents.

“To make things much worse, this obligation triggers on charging a person with a crime, not on a conviction,” he added.

Burton Brown disagreed, noting that nothing in Proposition 81 allows profiling or gives ICE agents any authority they don’t have in Colorado.

She added, “Instead, this gives Colorado law enforcement the ability to report violent criminals or repeat felons if they are here illegally without facing a $50,000 fine from the state.”

Walsh insisted that Proposition 81 would further erode the already strained relationship between immigrant communities and law enforcement.

“Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement,” he said. “If Proposition 81 passes, we would no longer be able to do that.”

Larimer and Jackson County District Attorney Gordon McLaughlin also attended the rally.

description:

Earlier this week, in a victory for DOJ, a federal judge in Kansas ruled that state’s tuition law unconstitutional.

text:
The U.S. Department of Justice sued Utah, the District of Columbia and two more states this week for granting in-state college tuition and scholarships to immigrants without permanent legal status. The cases are the latest in a push by the Trump administration to end the practice across the country.

The department’s attorneys argue the policies discriminate against U.S. citizens from out of state. The new cases, filed Thursday, bring the total to 25 lawsuits over allowing resident tuition for unauthorized immigrants in states where they live, the department said in a news release.

Earlier this week, in a victory for DOJ, a federal judge in Kansas ruled that state’s tuition law unconstitutional.

“No more placing illegal aliens over American citizens on this Department of Justice’s watch,” said Stanley Woodward Jr., associate U.S. attorney general, in a prepared statement.

The lawsuits follow President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive order directing the DOJ and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to take action against states’ enforcement of policies granting resident tuition to immigrants without legal authorization.

Utah allows in-state tuition for students who graduated in Utah after attending high school in the state for at least three years. Proponents of such policies say they don’t change any academic requirements and allow students to pay the same rate as the classmates they grew up with.

A legislative proposal seeking to end the benefit in Utah passed the House by a narrow margin but did not get a vote or sponsor in the Senate this year after opponents raised concerns it could make college unaffordable for students who have lived much of their lives in Utah.

State lawmakers are likely to continue the debate into next year. Top Republican legislators focused Thursday on the question of who taxpayer money should serve.

“Utah taxpayers should not be footing the bill for benefits extended to individuals who are here illegally. Our taxpayer dollars should prioritize Utah citizens,” House Speaker Mike Schultz said Friday in a statement to Utah News Dispatch. Schultz, R-Hooper, voted in favor of the 2026 measure.

“The Legislature has a responsibility to protect Utah taxpayers and make sure state resources are being used as intended,” Schultz said in the statement. “I look forward to addressing this issue and making the necessary changes during the 2027 General Session.”

Senate President Stuart Adams said Friday that he and his colleagues in the Senate were still reviewing the lawsuit. Adams seemed to reference tenets of Utah’s moderate 2010 immigration compact as he reflected on the state’s next steps, though he didn’t signal what they may look like.

“Utah has long valued those who come to this country legally, strengthen our communities and contribute to our economy. But taxpayer-funded benefits should prioritize those they are intended to serve,” Adams said in a prepared statement.

He said the Senate “is committed to protecting Utah taxpayers, respecting those who follow the legal immigration process and ensuring Utah law is fair, lawful and consistent with federal requirements.”

As of 2023, the state was home to an estimated 140,000 unauthorized immigrants, according to the Pew Research Center, though it wasn’t clear how many were of college age. Utah’s total population at the time was roughly 3.4 million.

DOJ’s lawsuit filed in federal court in Utah names the state, the Utah System of Higher Education and its commissioner, Geoffrey Landward, as defendants.

In an unsigned statement to Utah News Dispatch, the Utah System of Higher Education said “we support students who meet the eligibility requirements established in state law and defer to the Utah Legislature’s authority to set tuition policy for our public colleges and universities. We will continue to administer that in accordance with legislative direction.”

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown declined through a spokesperson to speak about the pending litigation that advocates condemned as shameful.

“This coordinated attack on the rights of young immigrants is unprecedented and unwarranted,” said Thomas Saenz, president of the Los Angeles-based Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, in a Friday statement. “No administration of either party has ever previously challenged these state tuition-equity laws.”

In-state tuition and fees at the flagship University of Utah is $10,480 for the current academic year, while non-resident tuition is $32,932, according to the university’s estimates. The exact cost varies based on a student’s specific program and coursework.
